title: Origins of microwave losses in superconducting circuits made with silicon-on-insulator substrates
authors: Simon Messelot, Nicolas Aparicio, Kazi Rafsanjani Amin, Eric Eyraud, Bruno Fain, Mikaël Cassé, Guillaume Jourdan, Fabrice Nemouchi, Sébastien Hentz, Frédéric Gustavo, François Lefloch, Nicolas Roch, Jérémie J. Viennot, Julien Renard
abstract: Silicon-on-insulator technology is widely used to fabricate silicon based devices, from advanced transistors to photonic circuits or nanomechanical systems. Integrating low loss superconducting quantum circuits with silicon-on-insulator substrates enables to couple the advantages offered by the mature silicon technology to the exquisite sensitivity of superconducting circuits. The natural approach, inherited from research in superconducting microwave devices, is to use a substrate made with highly resistive silicon, known for its low level of microwave losses. In this work, using superconducting microwave resonators, we show that counterintuitively, standard resistivity silicon-on-insulator substrates perform better than high resistivity silicon-on-insulator substrates at cryogenic temperatures. In the latter case, the presence of a parasitic sheet conduction at the interface between bulk silicon and silicon oxide acts as the dominant loss mechanism. This parasitic sheet can be suppressed using substrates with intentionally induced traps. In such substrates, losses are ultimately limited by the dielectric losses of the silicon oxide layer. These substrates offer interesting perspectives for the development of superconducting nanoelectromechanical systems. First, the release, i.e. the removal of the silicon oxide, could be limited to the moving parts, thereby maintaining the mechanical integrity of the rest of the device. Additionally, such structure would enhance heat evacuation into the bulk of the substrate which is an issue in current devices such as microwave-to-optics converters.
summary: This research analyzes microwave losses in superconducting circuits built on various SOI substrates. It reveals that high-resistivity silicon suffers from parasitic surface conduction loss at the $	ext{Si}/	ext{SiO}_2$ interface, while standard silicon is limited by doping. The authors show that engineering traps into the substrate can suppress these losses, leading to superior device performance.
main_problem: The study investigates the origins of microwave losses in superconducting circuits fabricated on Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) substrates at cryogenic temperatures.
main_result: Standard resistivity SOI performs counterintuitively better than high-resistivity SOI because the latter suffers from parasitic sheet conduction loss; trap-rich SOI offers the best performance by suppressing these interface losses.
method: Losses are characterized by measuring the internal quality factor ($Q_i$) of superconducting microwave resonators using $S_{21}$ measurements at base temperatures near 25 mK.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a superconducting resonator (TiN film) integrated onto various SOI substrates (Standard, High-Resistivity, Trap-rich). The analysis models loss mechanisms like parasitic sheet conduction and dielectric losses in the $	ext{SiO}_2$ layer.
key_observables: Internal quality factor ($Q_i$), $S_{21}$ scattering parameter, power dependence of $Q_i$, and temperature dependence of losses.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperatures ($\approx 25 	ext{ mK}$), substrate resistivity ($ho$), defect charge densities, and the presence/absence of parasitic sheet conduction (PSC).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that PSC is the dominant loss mechanism in high-resistivity substrates, and that losses in trap-rich SOI are ultimately limited by $	ext{SiO}_2$ dielectric losses.
figures_summary: Figures show typical resonance shapes ($S_{21}$ vs. Frequency) for different substrate types, illustrating the measured quality factors under various conditions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares four types of SOI substrates using microwave resonators to pinpoint the dominant loss mechanism—identifying PSC in HR-SOI and demonstrating superior performance with trap-induced traps.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it directly addresses material science limitations for superconducting quantum devices, which are central to building scalable quantum hardware architectures.
